speaker: jaycohen
text: So welcome to an oral argument session of the Fifth District Court of Appeal. As I indicated earlier, we are recording this on YouTube. So if you have any filters that you'd like to utilize, that's okay with me. I'm joined, I'm Jay Cohen, and I'll be presiding today. I'm joined on this panel by Judge Jim Edwards and Judge Meredith Sesso. It's my honor and your good fortune to have those folks joining us on this panel. We are set for United Automobile Insurance Company versus AFO Imaging, doing business as Advanced Diagnostic Group. That's 20-2442. Both sides will be entitled up to 20 minutes each for their oral arguments. The appellant may reserve time for rebuttal. The default on that is a five-minute rebuttal timeframe, but if you'd like something different than that, it's not a problem to accommodate whatever you would like. So that said, we are ready to proceed. Mr. Neiman. Thank you.

speaker: michaelneimand
text: Good morning, Your Honor. May it please the Court. I'll accept the default time, five minutes for rebuttal. That'll be fine for me. Thank you. All right. This is an appeal from a PIP case where the county court struck United Auto from the defense of material misrepresentation because it was asserted more than 30 days after the claim was reported. This issue has been resolved in United Auto versus Rodriguez in 2001, when the Florida Supreme Court held that the only penalty for denying a claim more than 30 days, or not paying a claim, rather, more than 30 days after it was noticed is that if the insurance company loses, they would have to pay the penalty of interest in attorney's fees. This court followed up with Rodriguez, which was an RRN case with January. And in January, this court was facing the issue of whether a claim that the coverage didn't exist because the car was not listed on the policy, was not a replacement policy, was not barred after 30 days because if there's no coverage, could there be a bar of the claim itself? In addition, the third district in United Auto versus Sato has held that section 409, which is the rescission section of the insurance code applies to PIP. And in PIP, it makes no difference because section 409 is the basic statute that imports the meeting of the minds contract provision, which says if the two parties did not know actually what they were agreeing to, there's no contract. And in this case, United Auto found out during the investigation that there was a misstatement. The misstatement was in the application where the insured said they owned the car during the EOO before their lawsuit was filed. It was determined that the person who said they owned the car and took the insurance out on the car was not the owner of the car.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: What is your response to the argument that the amendments to the statute, specifically subsection I or paragraph I, basically render the previous holding in Rodriguez obsolete and we should be looking at this as a-

speaker: michaelneimand
text: So if you look at the history of four I, there was a problem early on, and it's always been a problem as we know that if you're going to plead fraud, you have to plead with specificity. If you're gonna deny fraud, it's a specific intent crime, not crime, I'm a criminal lawyer, it's a specific intent offense. And therefore you didn't have enough time within the 30 days to do the investigation before you denied it. So the only purpose of four I, if it is in fact fraud, is to give the insurance company, the industry more time to investigate, to determine whether or not there's fraud and whether they're going to use it. The problem with that, to say that four I applies here and that's where I was going when I was talking about material misrepresentation defense, that's not a fraud defense. If we look at 409, it doesn't have to be fraud, it could be an unintentional misrepresentation. So the fact that this can't even be pled under fraud, this is not a fraudulent situation, this is just a material misrepresentation. And when an insurance company goes to prove the material misrepresentation, all they have to show is that the statement was false. They don't have to show there was any specific intent to defraud because the fact of the matter is that I was saying is that it's the fact that there's no meeting of the minds. The parties did not agree on the basic facts and the contract was entered factually. But even so, even if it would apply, not every case has to be done by that. If you look at the statute, it says, if the insurance company wants to, they have to file the letter with the Office of Insurance Regulation to enact this and then go forward with it. There's no way that that in any way, shape or form in the language of it, done anything other than to extend the time an insurance company has to investigate the claim. Because it says, after the claim is investigated within 90 days, you either have to pay it or if you deny it and you subsequently lose the case, you have to pay interest. And it goes back to what we said.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: If we agree with that argument, your requested remand instruction is for entry of summary judgment in favor of United Auto. Why would we not remand for additional consideration of that motion?

speaker: michaelneimand
text: Well, because as a summary judgment hearing, United Auto filed the affidavits of their adjuster and their underwriter to establish that the MM occurred, and it was a material, the amount of premiums and the premiums were returned. No affidavit was filed by the plaintiff at that proceeding. They went strictly on the issue of the issue of law. So they didn't defend on this. And therefore, if it goes back on the fact that 4I doesn't apply, well, then you'll be giving the plaintiff a second bite of the apple because nobody prevented them from defending on two grounds. They could have defended saying there's an issue of fact, and even if there is an issue of fact, it wouldn't matter as a matter of law. So since they did not file the necessary affidavits, I think United Auto is entitled to a summary judgment upon remand.

speaker: jaycohen
text: All right. Anything else, or do you want to reserve the remaining time for-

speaker: michaelneimand
text: I think this is a very straightforward argument. I think when we look at what Rodriguez has said, it applies to any defense, whether it's reasonably related, necessary, or any affirmative defense. The fact of the matter is an insurance company, the only penalty for not paying the claim within 30 days is if they lose, they have to pay interest in attorney's fees. And I'll reserve the rest of my rebuttal. Thank you.

speaker: jaycohen
text: All right. Thank you, sir. All right, Mr. Ostendorf.

speaker: danielosterndorf
text: Yes, good morning, Your Honor. May it please the court. I'm Daniel Ostendorf, counsel for Appalachia. I'd like to first start off with noting that the argument that section 627-409 and the Salgado case are applicable to any of the issues raised on appeal by the appellant, neither of them are relevant, nor can they be raised. The issue of rescission under section 627-409 was not raised by the appellant in its initial brief. It was only raised by the appellant in their reply brief. And so accordingly, as this court knows, it is incumbent upon the appellant to raise all issues that it intends to base an appeal on in the initial brief. If those issues are not raised in initial brief, they cannot be considered and are deemed abandoned. And this court is without power to revive them or resurrect those issues. So in terms of United Auto's argument that they had the right to rescind pursuant to section 627-409 or under the case on Salgado, they've lost that right. They've waived it, it's gone. In terms of the applicability of 627-7364I and the time requirements, the mandatory time requirements as set forth in the statute, they are applicable. And it's especially true in this case. So I think a brief, very brief timeline would be helpful to the court. The policy at issue was issued on July 7th of 2018.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: We're familiar with the facts. Can you explain how-

speaker: danielosterndorf
text: The key is that on October 4th of 2018, they conducted the EEO of Ruben Torres. That was done six days before they even received a bill from my client advanced diagnostic group. So the information that they had that they based their rescission on was already in their possession six days before they received a bill from my client. The entire purpose of the no fault statute as this court is well aware is to ensure swift and virtually automatic payment of PIP benefits. And it is to do so, so that people can get on with their lives without a financial interruption, whether that's the insureds or the assignee and their insureds. So in this particular case, the statute specifically requires generally under 4B that claims be paid or denied within 30 days. But as Judge Sassa has pointed out, subsequent to the January decision and the United Auto versus Rodriguez decision, the legislature went back and enacted 4I specifically for purposes of allowing an insurance carrier who had suspected fraud, which I believe is a distinguishment and a difference between a fraud and a material misrepresentation. And ultimately said, if you're going to conduct an investigation, this is how you have to do it. And this is when you have to do it. 4I says you have 30 days to conduct your investigation. If that's not enough time, you have the right to get more. You simply write a letter and you are given an additional 60 days. In this case-

speaker: meredithsasso
text: Doesn't that just extend the timeline for when payments become overdue?

speaker: danielosterndorf
text: Yes and no. Yes, payments are overdue and yes, penalties and interest would be due. However, Your Honor, I think it's also important to note that the requirement of this court is to read this statute as a whole in totality. In this case, to accept United Auto's argument that they are entitled to defend for any and all reasons at any time, whenever they so choose, flies in the face of the statutory language when you read all the paragraphs together. Specifically, if you look, the United Auto Rodriguez case says that there's nothing in the statute that prevents the insurance carrier from defending on a basis of reasonable, necessary, and related, which ultimately the legislature codified in 2001 into the statute. They added a specific provision that says that the insurance carrier never waives the right to argue reasonableness, necessity, or relatedness. So what can we glean from that? It's that the legislature knows how to write a provision in a statute that preserves a defense so that the insurance carrier cannot be held or be found to have waived it. Further, in 2013, they added 4I, which strengthened the requirements. It further established the requirements that the insurance carrier take certain acts under certain circumstances, which are those expressly in this particular case.

speaker: edwards
text: Counsel, did United claim fraud?

speaker: danielosterndorf
text: They claimed material misrepresentation in the application for the policy of insurance, and more specifically- Let me ask you again.

speaker: edwards
text: Let me ask you again. Did United ever claim fraud?

speaker: danielosterndorf
text: They did not use the word fraud. They claimed material misrepresentation.

speaker: edwards
text: 4I uses only the word fraud, doesn't it?

speaker: danielosterndorf
text: It does use fraud, Your Honor. It does.

speaker: edwards
text: How can you say fraud, material misrepresentation, are the same thing? They're not.

speaker: danielosterndorf
text: In most circumstances, they are separate and distinct. I think with regard to the purpose of the Pitt statute, which is the investigation of fraudulent or misrepresentation in claims, that it's a distinguished without a difference. Ultimately, the investigation is the same. But even if we assume that it's fraud only that 4I applies to, Your Honor, they still waive their ability to assert material misrep in this case. Why? Because even after the 2013 amendment to the statute that added 4I, the legislature did not add what I described as a savings clause to the Pitt statute the way they did when they added a savings clause for the argument as to reasonableness, necessity, or relatedness. The legislature knows how to write those savings clause in. They'd already done it when they added the paragraph in amendment 01, consistent with the United Auto versus Rodriguez decision.

speaker: meredithsasso
text: Doesn't the flip of your argument also apply that the legislature knows how to preclude and ensure from being able to certain defense? That's not here. So why, if you agree that this is an extension for the period of when payments become overdue, why would we not, as the Fuller Supreme Court did, interpret that only as an extension of when payments become overdue and not a provision precluding and ensure from asserting a defense or contesting?

speaker: danielosterndorf
text: Your Honor, Judge Jessup, I think it's because you have to. Because when you read the statute together as a totality and give force and effect to all of its provisions, including 4B, you have to read the statute as a whole and see that where the legislature wants to preserve the insurance carrier's right to assert particular defenses beyond the 30-day time period as set forth, which is a mandatory time period, they knew how to write that in and they did it. They didn't add in their fraud, material misrepresentation. They didn't add in anything other than reasonable, necessary, and related. So because they omitted the fraud or material misrep, the court, in construing the statute, is required to conclude that they knew what they were doing when they omitted it and not engraft that language onto the statute. It's simply enforce the statute, the clear and unambiguous language of 4B as it is written. And again, I think if you look to the policy behind what is the whole purpose of the statute, which is where I started, the purpose of the statute is to ensure timely and virtually automatic payment of benefits. To subscribe to the theory put forth in both its brief and reply brief by United Auto is that they can do whatever they want, whenever they want, and however they want it. And what kind of a burden does then that place on insureds or assignee of insureds? Hey, listen, we didn't pay on time. We know a statute says we're supposed to do it. We didn't do it. You now, you gotta send us another demand letter. You're gonna have to file suit against us because we're gonna sit back and not pay anything because we now know that we can just do whatever we want, whenever we want, however we want, and raise any defense that we think is appropriate, whenever we think it's appropriate to raise that a defense. That's not what the statute says. The statute requires you do certain things within certain time periods. And if you don't do them, and especially in this case, where the defense, I'm sorry, the insurer is in possession of the information that they use to rescind this policy before they even receive a bill from my client. And yet they took no action whatsoever for 55 days, 61 if you count when they took the examination under oath of Mr. Torres. When you're in possession of that information and you have the ability to make a decision, they took that EUO for a reason. They suspected something was wrong, and yet they chose to take no action with that information in their possession. That's a waiver. And if you read that in accordance with the provisions of the statutes, where all of them need to be read together, 4B, 4I, they didn't comply with that statute provision, they didn't comply with the timelines, it's admitted. Ultimately, that argument, they've waived the ability to raise those defenses. They've, the statute says what it says, and this court is just simply required to enforce it as written. And with that, I've concluded. I don't know that there's anything else unless the panel has additional questions for me.

speaker: jaycohen
text: All right, thank you, sir. All right, Mr. Neiman. Thank you, Your Honors.

speaker: michaelneimand
text: I hear this a lot of times in a reply brief when I raise an issue that addresses other issues in the answer brief, that I'm barred from raising it up. The whole issue here is material misrepresentation. The whole issue is the interpretation of the statute. So I believe clearly Sousato applies, and I'm allowed to raise it. The interesting thing about the 6B analysis of RRN, when Rodriguez was going through, the industry was very afraid that it was gonna lose Rodriguez. And that amendment to 6B that said that you could raise RRN at any time was passed by the legislature before the Supreme Court ruled on Rodriguez. You could see that just by going through that. So I don't think that analysis applies, because when you go to look at the holding in Rodriguez, the court emphasized, quotes, that nothing in the statute provides that once payment becomes overdue, the insurer is forever barred from contesting the claim. They didn't say contesting the claim on RRN. They didn't say specifically limit to anything. They said not to contest the claim. And to allow this interpretation to do away with the right to rescind on the material misrepresentation is to enforce the insurance company to accept a contract under terms and conditions it never would have agreed to. And that's the whole purpose of 409. The argument that the insurance company could do anything they want forever and ever, and the poor insured has no ramifications, that argument was made in Rodriguez. And the court said, the way that we resolve that is we punish the insurer. And that is, if he does all this and he still loses the insurer, he's subject to attorney's fees. And I don't know what the rates are in your district, but in my district, a two or three year lawyer gets 200 or $300 an hour to PIP, anywhere up to 800, $900 an hour for more seasoned lawyers. And for litigating a PIP case with the benefits of $10,000 and paying out 40 to 50 to $100,000 in attorney's fees because the insurer was wrong, I think that's a big penalty. And insurer has to really make certain that they're doing the right thing. That's why it takes time to not only find out when we're investigating claim that there's a possible MM, but we have to be actually sure that the facts are true and that a material misrepresentation did occur because if we aren't sure and we're going forward to that, we're opening up ourselves to a very great liability for attorney's fees. So this virtual automatic and swift payment has been used over and over and over and over again. And I've been doing PIP since 2004 and this has been a God, I don't know how many years I've been hearing that before that. But the swift payment doesn't allow the insured to commit a wrongdoing, whether intentional or otherwise. And then the insurance company would still have to be on the hook. Again, and I look at this and I don't wanna beat a dead horse because I've been beating it for a while. But if you look at Rodriguez, it's very, very clear. If you look at 4I, the language is 4I, it doesn't do anything to Rodriguez. If you look at your court's decision in January, following Rodriguez, it all makes sense. It all puts it right out there, following the law to allow an insurance company to defend a claim in any way they see fit, subject to, if they lose it, the penalties that they're gonna have to pay interest on the benefits and they will be subject to attorney's fees. On that ground, I believe that this court should reverse. And as I stated in my direct, since the plaintiff did not file any affidavits against the actual material misrepresentation that occurred that were filed by United Audit by its underwriter and its litigation justice, that this court should reverse with instructions to enter a final judgment in favor of United Audit on the front of the defense of material misrepresentation. Thank you very much, Your Honor. All right, thank you both for your arguments and we'll be in recess.

speaker: jaycohen
text: Thank you, Your Honor.
